# A different kind of combining

## Last time: counting deprivations

Last session we built our own poverty index.

We counted how many things each student lacked, and by how much.

## This time: no counting

Today nobody is simply deprived or not deprived.

We have continuous measurements, in completely different units.

## The real world problem

Countries are compared on life expectancy, years of schooling, and income.

Years, years, and rupees or dollars. Very different units.

## The Human Development Index

The Human Development Index, or HDI, solves exactly this problem [@hdr2020tech].

It turns three very different measurements into one score between 0 and 1.

## Same two building blocks, one difference

We still need to pick our dimensions and pick a way to combine them.

But there is no poor or non-poor split this time. Everyone gets a score.

# Meet the class, again

## The same six students

Aditi, Zara, Rohan, Kabir, Meera, and Dev.

This time we ask a different question about them.

## Not "who lacks what"

Instead we ask: how well is each student doing, on a continuous scale?

## Three dimensions, HDI style

HDI uses three dimensions: a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living [@hdr2020tech].

We will use a classroom version of each.

## Our three dimensions {.smaller}

**A healthy routine**: how many school days a student actually attends.

**Knowledge**: a vocabulary score, and books read for pleasure.

**Standard of living**: weekly pocket money.

# Step 1: The raw data

## Four things we measure

Days present out of 200 school days.

A vocabulary test score out of 50.

Books read this year.

Weekly pocket money, in rupees.

# Step 2: The normalization problem

## We cannot just add these up

190 days plus 45 points plus ₹300 means nothing on its own.

Days, test points, and rupees are not the same kind of thing.

## HDI's solution

Turn every raw number into an index between 0 and 1 first.

Only then combine the indices.

## Fixed reference points

To do this, HDI sets a minimum and a maximum for each indicator [@hdr2020tech].

These are called goalposts.

## Goalposts are normative, again

The minimum is a realistic floor. The maximum is an aspirational target.

Just like our deprivation cutoffs last session, someone had to choose these.

## The normalization formula

$$\text{Index} = \frac{\text{actual value} - \text{minimum}}{\text{maximum} - \text{minimum}}$$

This rescales any raw number onto a common 0 to 1 scale.

# Step 3: Setting our goalposts

## Choosing sensible bounds {.smaller}

Days present: floor of 120 days, aspirational target of 195 days.

Vocabulary score: floor of 0, maximum possible score of 50.

Books read: floor of 0, aspirational target of 40 books a year.

Pocket money: floor of ₹10 a week, aspirational target of ₹500 a week.

# Step 4: The health dimension

## The simplest case

Days present only needs one indicator.

We apply the normalization formula directly.

## Aditi's health index, worked out

$$\text{Health}_{\text{Aditi}} = \frac{190 - 120}{195 - 120} = \frac{70}{75} \approx 0.933$$

Aditi attends school almost as often as our aspirational target.

## Dev's health index, worked out

$$\text{Health}_{\text{Dev}} = \frac{130 - 120}{195 - 120} = \frac{10}{75} \approx 0.133$$

Dev is much closer to our floor of 120 days.

# Step 5: The knowledge dimension

## Two indicators this time

Knowledge has both a vocabulary score and a books-read count.

Each needs its own index first.

## Normalize the vocabulary score

$$\text{Vocabulary index} = \frac{\text{score} - 0}{50 - 0}$$

## Normalize books read

$$\text{Books index} = \frac{\text{books} - 0}{40 - 0}$$

## Combining the two sub-indices

HDI combines the two schooling-type indicators with a plain arithmetic mean [@hdr2020tech].

$$\text{Knowledge} = \frac{\text{Vocabulary index} + \text{Books index}}{2}$$

## Why an arithmetic mean here

An arithmetic mean lets one sub-indicator make up for the other [@hdr2020tech].

A student strong in vocabulary but light on reading can still land in the middle.

# Step 6: The standard of living dimension

## Money behaves differently

Pocket money could be normalized the same simple way.

But HDI treats income differently, on purpose [@hdr2020tech].

## Diminishing returns

An extra ₹50 means a lot to a student with ₹40 a week.

That same ₹50 means far less to a student who already has ₹300 a week.

## The natural logarithm

To capture this, HDI takes the natural log of income before normalizing [@hdr2020tech].

$$\text{Income index} = \frac{\ln(\text{actual}) - \ln(\text{minimum})}{\ln(\text{maximum}) - \ln(\text{minimum})}$$

## Kabir's income index, worked out

$$\text{Income}_{\text{Kabir}} = \frac{\ln(200) - \ln(10)}{\ln(500) - \ln(10)} \approx 0.766$$

Kabir's pocket money looks modest in rupees, but scores fairly high after logging.

# Step 7: Putting the three together

## The final aggregation step

HDI combines the three dimension indices with a geometric mean [@hdr2020tech].

$$\text{HDI} = \left(\text{Health} \times \text{Knowledge} \times \text{Income}\right)^{1/3}$$

## Aditi's HDI, worked out

$$\text{HDI}_{\text{Aditi}} = \left(0.933 \times 0.825 \times 0.869\right)^{1/3} \approx 0.875$$

## Ranking our class

```{r}
#| label: fig-hdi-ranking
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4

library(ggplot2)

students <- c("Aditi", "Zara", "Rohan", "Kabir", "Meera", "Dev")
hdi <- c(0.875, 0.649, 0.421, 0.494, 0.323, 0.187)   # from the table above

df <- data.frame(student = students, hdi = hdi)
df <- df[order(df$hdi), ]
df$student <- factor(df$student, levels = df$student)
df$label <- sprintf("%.3f", df$hdi)

ggplot(df, aes(x = student, y = hdi)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#044191", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.2, size = 6, colour = "#1f2933") +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "HDI") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

# Step 8: Why a geometric mean?

## A different way to average

We could have just averaged the three indices instead.

$$\text{Arithmetic mean} = \frac{\text{Health} + \text{Knowledge} + \text{Income}}{3}$$

## Look closely at Kabir

Kabir's three indices are uneven: 0.600, 0.263, and 0.766.

Strong in health and income, weak in knowledge.

## Two ways to average Kabir's scores

<div>
<div class="subgroup-box section-a"><strong>Arithmetic mean</strong><br>$(0.600+0.263+0.766)/3$<br>$\approx 0.543$</div>
<div class="subgroup-box section-b"><strong>Geometric mean</strong><br>$(0.600 \times 0.263 \times 0.766)^{1/3}$<br>$\approx 0.494$</div>
</div>

## What this shows

The geometric mean gives Kabir a lower score than the arithmetic mean.

A weak dimension pulls the geometric mean down more than a simple average.

Being strong in two dimensions cannot fully cover for being weak in a third.

# Step 9: Scoring the whole class

## A natural next question

Individual scores are useful. But what is our class's overall HDI?

## The tempting shortcut

We could just average everyone's HDI scores together.

$$\text{Naive class HDI} = \frac{0.875+0.649+0.421+0.494+0.323+0.187}{6} \approx 0.491$$

## That shortcut is not how HDI is aggregated

Official HDI group figures are not an average of individual HDI values [@hdr2020tech].

Instead, the raw indicators are averaged first, and the HDI formula is applied once, to those averages [@hdr2020tech].

## Averaging the raw indicators first

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th class="rowlabel">Indicator</th><th>Days present</th><th>Vocabulary score</th><th>Books read</th><th>Pocket money</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td class="rowlabel">Class average</td><td>158.3</td><td>25.0</td><td>11.8</td><td>₹138.3</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Recomputing HDI from these averages

$$\text{Health} = 0.511, \quad \text{Knowledge} = 0.398, \quad \text{Income} = 0.672$$

$$\text{Correct class HDI} = (0.511 \times 0.398 \times 0.672)^{1/3} \approx 0.515$$

## Two answers, side by side

<div>
<div class="subgroup-box section-a"><strong>Naive shortcut</strong><br>average of individual HDIs<br>$\approx 0.491$</div>
<div class="subgroup-box section-b"><strong>Correct method</strong><br>HDI of the class averages<br>$\approx 0.515$</div>
</div>

The two methods do not agree.

## Why they disagree

HDI mixes a logarithm and a geometric mean.

Neither of those treats an average of outputs the same as the output of an average.

## The takeaway for policy

Never average already-computed HDI values across a population.

Average the underlying indicators first, then apply the HDI formula once.

## A contrast worth noticing

Our gMPI last session could be split by section using a simple population-share sum.

HDI cannot be split that way. It must be rebuilt from the raw indicators each time.

# From our classroom to the real HDI

## Checking our formula on a real country

The technical note itself works through an example: Sudan [@hdr2020tech].

We can run Sudan's numbers through our own formula and see if we agree.

## Sudan's raw indicators {.smaller}

Life expectancy at birth: 65.3 years.

Expected years of schooling: 7.9 years.

Mean years of schooling: 3.8 years.

Gross national income per capita: $3,829 [@hdr2020tech].

## The real HDI goalposts {.smaller}

Life expectancy: floor of 20 years, target of 85 years.

Expected years of schooling: floor of 0, target of 18 years.

Mean years of schooling: floor of 0, target of 15 years.

Income per capita: floor of \$100, target of \$75,000 [@hdr2020tech].

## Computing Sudan's dimension indices

$$\text{Health} \approx 0.697, \qquad \text{Education} \approx 0.346, \qquad \text{Income} \approx 0.551$$

Education is the average of the expected and mean schooling indices.

## Sudan's HDI, our way

$$\text{HDI}_{\text{Sudan}} = (0.697 \times 0.346 \times 0.551)^{1/3} \approx 0.510$$

The technical note reports 0.510 for Sudan [@hdr2020tech].

## Small gaps are just rounding

Our figure differs from the technical note only in the third decimal place.

That gap comes from rounding the published inputs, not from a different formula.

## Where Sudan sits

Human development categories: very high from 0.800, high from 0.700, medium from 0.550, and low below that [@hdr2020tech].

At 0.510, Sudan falls into the low human development category.

# Recap

## What we built today

We turned four raw numbers into three dimension indices using fixed goalposts.

We used an arithmetic mean within knowledge, and a log transform for income.

We combined all three with a geometric mean to get HDI.

## What we learned about aggregating groups

A population's HDI is not the average of its members' HDI values.

It comes from re-averaging the raw indicators, then applying the formula once.
